runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?
runs.reply:
The best messaging app depends on your top priorities: who you chat with, privacy needs, required features, and your device ecosystem. Below are recommendations sorted by common use cases:
---
### 1. Best for General Use (cross-platform, matches most contacts)
These are ideal if you want to chat with friends/family who already use popular mainstream apps:
- **WhatsApp**: The most widely used messaging app globally. All 1:1 and group chats are end-to-end encrypted (E2EE) by default, with a simple interface, voice/video calls, file sharing, and status updates. The main downside is that it is owned by Meta, which collects non-message metadata (e.g., contact lists, usage patterns) for ad targeting. It requires a phone number to sign up.
- **Telegram**: Far more feature-rich than WhatsApp, with support for groups of up to 200,000 members, public broadcast channels (for following creators, brands, or news), custom stickers, automation bots, and cloud sync across all your devices. Note that only 1:1 "Secret Chats" are E2EE; regular group and cloud chats are not encrypted, as messages are stored on Telegram's servers. It also lets you sign up with a username instead of a phone number for more privacy.
- **Google Messages (Android + cross-platform with iPhone)**: The default SMS/RCS app for Android, now fully compatible with iMessage on iOS 18+. You can send high-quality photos, read receipts, and typing indicators to iPhone users without needing third-party apps, and all RCS chats are E2EE. It’s a low-fuss option for Android users who don’t want to add another app.
- **iMessage**: The seamless pick if all your contacts use Apple devices. All chats are E2EE by default, sync across iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch, and support features like message reactions, Apple Pay, and shared media playlists. It has no official Android support.
- **WeChat**: Dominant in China and among Chinese diaspora communities, it is a super-app combining messaging, mobile payments, food delivery, ride-hailing, and social media feeds. It is not recommended for privacy-sensitive use, as it has heavy government censorship and surveillance.
---
### 2. Best for Privacy & Security
Choose these if keeping your conversations private is your top priority:
- **Signal**: The gold standard for private messaging. All 1:1, group, and voice/video chats are E2EE by default, it is fully open-source, shows no ads, and collects only minimal metadata (your sign-up date and, if you choose, your phone number). As of 2024, you can also use a username instead of sharing your phone number with contacts. It has fewer extra features than mainstream apps, and no support for large public channels, but it is the most trusted option for sensitive conversations.
- **Session**: Even more privacy-focused than Signal, with no phone number required to sign up. It uses decentralized onion routing with no central servers, so there is no single point of failure for data breaches or government subpoenas. All chats are E2EE by default. The tradeoff is low adoption, so you may have trouble convincing contacts to switch.
- **Threema**: A paid (one-time $5 fee) Swiss-based app with no phone number required, E2EE for all chats, and open-source code. It is not subject to U.S./EU data laws, making it a good pick for privacy-focused users who want a more polished interface than Session. The paywall limits widespread adoption.
---
### 3. Best for Work & Team Collaboration
- **Slack**: The most popular team chat tool, with organized channels for different projects/teams, integrations with hundreds of work tools (Google Drive, Asana, GitHub, etc.), threaded conversations to reduce chat clutter, and file sharing. The free tier limits message history to 90 days.
- **Microsoft Teams**: Seamless for companies that use Microsoft 365, with native integration to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook, plus support for large enterprise-grade video meetings and security controls. It can feel clunky for small teams.
- **Mattermost**: An open-source, self-hostable team chat tool perfect for companies that want to keep all internal communications on their own servers for maximum security. It is highly customizable and integrates with most common work tools.
- **Discord**: Also popular for small creative, gaming, or startup teams, with low-latency chat, voice channels for quick calls, screen sharing, and easy-to-set-up private servers.
---
### 4. Best for Communities & Large Groups
- **Discord**: The go-to for hobby, gaming, fan, and creator communities. It supports servers with hundreds of thousands of members, live voice/video channels for events, custom moderation bots, and low-latency chat for gaming. As of 2024, DMs, voice, and video chats are E2EE, though server text chats are not yet.
- **Telegram**: Ideal for large public broadcast channels (which can have millions of subscribers) and big group chats. Many news outlets, creators, and brands use Telegram to share updates with followers.
- **Circle**: Built specifically for paid creator communities, course groups, and membership spaces. It has robust moderation tools, integrated payment support for paid tiers, discussion threads, and live event hosting, making it perfect for professional, paid communities.
---
### Quick Tip
If you’re unsure, start with the app most of your existing contacts already use to avoid fragmentation. Switch to a specialized app only if you have specific needs (e.g., privacy for sensitive conversations, team collaboration tools). No app is 100% risk-free: always avoid sharing highly sensitive information even on E2EE platforms, as metadata or device compromise can still create risks.

runs.reply:
As an AI, I don’t have personal accounts or daily communication needs, so this is based on balancing usability, security, and real-world compatibility for typical user priorities—plus what I’d choose for my own hypothetical use as a regular person, with tradeoffs clearly laid out:

---
### My picks by core use case:
#### 1. For everyday personal use (friends, family, low friction, maximum contact compatibility)
- If you (and most of your contacts) use Apple devices: **iMessage** is the clear pick. It’s seamless across all Apple hardware, has default end-to-end encryption (E2EE) for all chats, requires no extra app downloads, and supports all the standard features people expect (reactions, read receipts, high-quality media sharing). The only downside is no official Android support, so you’ll need a fallback for Android-using contacts.
- If you need cross-platform compatibility (mix of Android/iPhone contacts): **WhatsApp** is my go-to here. It’s the most widely used messaging app globally, so almost everyone already has it, all 1:1 and group chats have default E2EE, and it’s extremely simple to use. The tradeoff is that it’s owned by Meta, which collects non-message metadata (contact lists, usage patterns, etc.) for ad targeting, so it’s not ideal if you’re wary of that. If Meta’s data practices are a dealbreaker, **Google Messages** (for Android users) is a great alternative: it now supports full RCS compatibility with iMessage on iOS 18+, has default E2EE for all RCS chats, and no extra app is needed for iPhone users.

#### 2. If privacy/security is a top priority (sensitive conversations, activism, journalism, etc.)
**Signal**, no question. It’s the most trusted privacy-focused messaging app: fully open-source, independently audited, default E2EE for all 1:1 chats, groups, and voice/video calls, collects almost no metadata (only your sign-up date, and you can use a username instead of your phone number as of 2024), no ads, and no data selling. The only downside is smaller user adoption, so you’ll need to convince close contacts to switch for it to be useful for sensitive chats.

#### 3. For work/team collaboration
- If your company uses Microsoft 365: **Microsoft Teams**, no question. It integrates natively with all Microsoft Office tools, has enterprise-grade security controls, and supports large-scale video meetings.
- For small teams, startups, or creative groups: **Discord**. It’s far less clunky than Slack or Teams, has low-latency voice channels for quick calls, easy server setup for different projects, and lots of customization. It’s also free for most small team use cases.
- If your team needs fully self-hosted, on-premise communication for maximum security: **Mattermost**, the open-source, self-hostable alternative to Slack.

#### 4. For communities and large group use
- For hobby, gaming, fan, or creator communities: **Discord** is the clear pick, with support for servers of any size, live voice/video events, custom moderation bots, and low-latency chat.
- For large public broadcast channels (news, creator updates, brand announcements): **Telegram**, which supports channels with millions of subscribers and has no limits on broadcast audience size.
- For paid creator/membership communities: **Circle**, which has built-in payment processing, tiered membership support, and moderation tools built specifically for paid community spaces.

---

I’d use iMessage for casual chats with my Apple-using friends and family, Signal for any sensitive conversations with people who also have it, Discord for my gaming hobby groups, and Slack for work. I’d avoid Telegram for regular private chats unless I’m using its E2EE Secret Chats feature, since standard cloud chats are not end-to-end encrypted, and I’d only use WeChat if I lived in China and needed its super-app features, due to its heavy censorship and surveillance risks.

runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?

The best messaging app depends entirely on your specific priorities (privacy, who you’re contacting, region, extra features, etc.). Below are top recommendations sorted by common use cases:

---

### 1. Best for General, Wide Compatibility: WhatsApp
- **Pros**: With over 2 billion global users, nearly all your contacts will already have it. It uses default end-to-end encryption (E2EE) for all 1:1 and group messages, calls, and shared media. It works on iOS, Android, desktop, and web, supports group chats of up to 1024 people, and uses data rather than SMS, so you won’t incur international messaging fees when traveling.
- **Cons**: Owned by Meta, so it collects user metadata (contact lists, chat timestamps, usage patterns) even with E2EE enabled. It requires a linked phone number to sign up, and is blocked in some regions (e.g., China, Iran, Russia). Desktop access requires your primary phone to stay connected to the internet.

---

### 2. Best for Features & Multi-Device Access: Telegram

#### Europe
- **Bolt**: The top budget pick, usually 10-20% cheaper than Uber across most EU countries, with wide coverage in Western, Eastern, and Northern Europe. It supports international cards and has an English interface.
- **Free Now (formerly MyTaxi)**: Best for regulated, licensed taxi rides, owned by major auto brands. All drivers are certified taxi operators, with transparent metered fares and minimal hidden surge pricing in most areas. It is especially popular in Germany, the UK, Spain, and Italy.

#### Asia
- **Southeast Asia (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Philippines, etc.)**: **Grab** is the dominant all-in-one super app, offering ride-hailing, food delivery, payments, and bike/scooter rentals.   - India: **Ola** is the most popular local option, with wider coverage in smaller tier 2/3 cities, and support for local payment methods like UPI. Uber also operates widely in major Indian cities.

  - China: **Didi Chuxing** is the only major player (Uber exited the Chinese market). It has an English interface for tourists, accepts international credit cards, and lets you pre-book cross-border rides for arrivals.

- **Tourist Use**: Grab (Southeast Asia), Didi (China), or Uber (global) – all have English interfaces, support international credit cards, and many offer tourist-focused support like in-app translation.

- Confirm payment options: Tourists should ensure the app accepts international credit cards; locals may prefer apps that support regional mobile wallets (UPI in India, Kakao Pay in South Korea, etc.).
- Compare estimated fares before booking, and be aware of surge pricing during peak hours, bad weather, or large events.
- If you’re traveling to a region with loose ride-hailing regulation, opt for apps that connect to licensed taxis (like Free Now) for added fare transparency and safety.

runs.u: Can you recommend a ride-hailing app?
runs.reply:
Ride-hailing app recommendations depend heavily on your location, as most services are region-specific. Below is a breakdown of the best options by major market, plus niche picks for specific use cases:

### By Region
#### North America (US, Canada)
- **Uber**: The most widely available option, covering all major and most smaller cities, with a full range of vehicle types (economy, premium, shared, wheelchair-accessible).
- **Lyft**: A strong competitor, often slightly cheaper for short trips, with a more localized customer service experience and popular shared ride options.
- **Curb**: Connects directly to licensed city taxis, with regulated, fixed fares and no surge pricing in most areas, ideal for users who prefer official taxi services.
- Niche: *Via* for affordable shared fixed-route rides in major cities like NYC, Chicago, and DC; *Blacklane* for premium airport/executive transfers.

#### Europe
- **Bolt**: The most popular budget option across the EU/EEA, UK, and Scandinavia, typically 20-30% cheaper than Uber, with wide coverage in both Western and Eastern Europe.
- **Free Now (formerly mytaxi)**: Backed by BMW and Mercedes, it partners exclusively with licensed local taxis, offering highly regulated service, fixed fares in many cities, and no hidden fees.
- **Uber**: Available in most major European cities, a good pick for consistent service if you use the app globally.
- Niche: *Addison Lee* (UK) for premium rides; local municipal taxi apps (e.g. in London, Paris) for direct regulated taxi bookings.
- *CIS (Russia, Kazakhstan, etc.)*: **Yandex Go** is the dominant local option, integrated with Yandex's maps and payment ecosystem, and far more reliable than Uber in the region.

#### East Asia
- **Japan**: **GO (formerly JapanTaxi)** is the market leader, connecting to all licensed local taxis, with an English interface and support for foreign credit cards. Uber is only available for limited luxury/taxi bookings here.
- **South Korea**: **Kakao T** is the go-to app, integrated with Kakao's ecosystem (KakaoPay, maps, messaging), covering all major cities and supporting foreign payment methods.
- **China**: **DiDi Chuxing** is the overwhelming market leader, with options for economy, premium, shared rides, and even micro-mobility (bikes/scooters). *Meituan* is a popular budget alternative with lower fares for short trips. Both support international credit cards for foreign users.

#### Southeast Asia
- **Grab**: The regional super app, dominant across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines. It offers ride-hailing, food delivery, payments, and parcel delivery, with English support and multiple payment options.
- **Gojek**: Indonesia's homegrown super app, also operating in Vietnam, Thailand, and Singapore. It is often cheaper than Grab for local trips in Indonesia and integrates with local e-wallets.
- **Bolt**: A fast-growing budget alternative in Thailand, Singapore, and Malaysia.

#### South Asia & MENA
- **India**: **Ola** is the most widely used local option, covering nearly all tier 1/2 cities, with added options for auto-rickshaws, bikes, and shared rides. Uber is also available but has less localized features.
- **MENA (Middle East & North Africa)**: **Careem** (owned by Uber but operates independently) is the regional leader, popular in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, and other MENA markets, with premium and economy options and multi-language support.
- **Pakistan/Bangladesh**: *Bykea* is a popular local low-cost option for rides and bike deliveries, alongside Careem and Uber.
- **Africa**: Bolt and InDriver are the most widely available options across major cities, alongside Uber in larger markets like South Africa, Nigeria, and Kenya.

#### Latin America
- **Uber**: Available in nearly all major LATAM countries, a consistent pick for international travelers.
- **Cabify**: Popular in Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Peru, and Spain, focusing on regulated licensed vehicles with higher quality than budget Uber options.
- **99 (owned by DiDi)**: Dominant in Brazil, also operating in Colombia, Ecuador, and other LATAM countries, with very affordable local fares.
- **InDriver**: Available across much of LATAM, with a unique feature that lets you negotiate fares directly with drivers to avoid surge pricing, great for budget travelers.

---

### Niche Use Cases
- **Budget shared rides**: *Via* (global in major cities), *InDriver* (emerging markets), *Bolt* (Europe/SEA)
- **Licensed taxi-only**: Curb (North America), Free Now (Europe), GO (Japan), Kakao T (South Korea)
- **Luxury/airport transfers**: Blacklane (global), Uber Premium/Lyft Lux, Careem Premium (MENA)
- **Micro-mobility (bikes/scooters)**: Most regional super apps (Grab, Gojek, DiDi, Ola) offer these options alongside car rides.

---

### Key Considerations When Choosing
1. **Local coverage**: Confirm the app operates in your specific city, as coverage can vary even within a country.
2. **Payment options**: Many local apps in emerging markets only accept local payment methods unless you are a resident, so prioritize apps that support international credit cards, Apple/Google Pay if you are traveling.
3. **Safety**: Pick apps with features like real-time trip sharing, driver background checks, in-app emergency buttons, and partnerships with licensed fleets if you prioritize regulated service.
4. **Pricing**: Compare base fares and surge pricing policies; budget regional apps are often 20-40% cheaper than Uber in their home markets.

For travelers, you can also use your hotel concierge to book pre-paid taxis to avoid surge pricing and language barriers in markets where local apps do not support foreign payment methods.

runs.reply:
The best ride-hailing app depends heavily on your location, budget, and specific needs (e.g. accessibility, luxury, safety features). Below are top recommendations broken down by region, plus cross-regional niche picks:

### By Major Region
#### North America (US, Canada)
1. **Uber**: The most widely available option, covering nearly all mid-to-large cities. It offers a full range of tiers: budget UberX, extra-legroom Uber Comfort, luxury Uber Black, and carpooling Uber Pool. It has robust safety features (trip sharing, in-app emergency button, driver background checks) and integrates with food delivery (Uber Eats) if needed.
2. **Lyft**: Uber’s main local rival, often with slightly lower base fares in many markets. It has similar standard and premium tiers, a reputation for more driver-friendly policies, and discounted ride programs for low-income users (Lyft Up). Safety features include real-time ride monitoring and 24/7 emergency support.
3. *Budget niche*: **Via** for shared fixed-route rides in major cities (NYC, Chicago, LA), which are far cheaper than standard ride-hailing for solo commuters.

#### Europe
1. **Bolt**: The top budget pick across most of the EU, with fares often 20-30% lower than Uber. It covers 40+ European countries, with options for standard rides, extra-legroom Bolt Comfort, and 6-seater Bolt XL for groups.
2. **Free Now (formerly MyTaxi)**: The leading licensed taxi hailing app in Germany, Spain, Italy, Greece and other markets. It connects you to regulated, metered taxis with no surprise surge pricing, ideal if you prefer official taxi services over private rides.
3. *Local picks*: **Yandex Go** dominates in Russia, Kazakhstan and other post-Soviet states; **Addison Lee** is a premium, reliable option for airport transfers and business travel in the UK.

#### Asia-Pacific
1. **Southeast Asia (Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Philippines, Vietnam)**: **Grab** is the undisputed leader—a "super app" that offers ride-hailing (standard, premium, licensed taxis, plus cheap bike/scooter rides for short trips), food delivery, grocery delivery, and digital payments. **Gojek** is a popular alternative in Indonesia and Singapore, often with lower fares for standard rides.
2. **China**: **Didi Chuxing** is the only app you’ll need, with coverage in every city. It offers budget Express rides, mid-range Premier, luxury Luxe, plus integrated bike-sharing, carpooling and food delivery. Uber has almost no presence in China after selling its local operations to Didi.
3. **Japan**: **GO (formerly JapanTaxi)** is the national standard for licensed taxis, with coverage in all cities, advance booking options, and app-based payment. Uber is only available for premium rides in Tokyo and Osaka.
4. **South Korea**: **Kakao T** (part of the Kakao messaging ecosystem) is the most widely used option, with access to taxis, private rides, carpooling, and integrated KakaoPay payments.
5. **India**: **Ola** is the local leader, with coverage in nearly all cities, budget Micro rides, premium Prime, and even auto-rickshaw booking for short trips. Uber is also widely available and often price-competitive.
6. **Australia/New Zealand**: Both Uber and **DiDi** are widely available, with DiDi often offering lower fares and new-user discounts.

#### Latin America
1. **Uber** operates in nearly all major markets (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, etc.).
2. **Cabify** is popular in Mexico, Peru, Colombia and Chile, with slightly higher fares but more professional drivers and stronger safety ratings, making it a good pick for business travel.
3. **DiDi** is expanding rapidly across the region, especially in Brazil and Mexico, with frequent discounts that make it cheaper than Uber in most cities.

#### Middle East & Africa
1. **Careem** (owned by Uber but operates independently in most markets) is the most trusted option across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, and parts of Africa (Kenya, Pakistan). It offers women-only ride options in many countries for extra safety, and supports local payment methods.
2. **Bolt** is a low-cost alternative expanding quickly across African cities (Lagos, Nairobi, Johannesburg).
3. Uber is also available in most major urban centers in the region.

---

### Cross-Regional Niche Picks
- **Luxury/airport transfers**: *Blacklane*, available in 50+ countries, offers fixed-fare premium rides with professional drivers, no surge pricing, and advance booking, ideal for business trips or airport pickups.
- **Accessibility**: Uber and Lyft have the most robust wheelchair-accessible vehicle (WAV) options in North America and Europe; local licensed taxi apps (e.g. Free Now, GO) often also offer accessible rides in their markets.
- **Women’s safety**: Beyond Careem’s women-only rides, many local apps (e.g. She Taxis in India, LadyBug Rides in parts of Africa) cater specifically to female riders.

---

### Quick Tips for Choosing
1. Download 2-3 apps for your destination to compare fares before booking, as prices can vary widely even in the same city.
2. Avoid surge pricing by booking in advance during peak hours, rush hour, or major events.
3. Prioritize apps with clear safety features (trip sharing, emergency support, driver verification) if you are traveling alone.

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
The best news outlet for you will depend on your location, topic interests, tolerance for editorial slant, and preferred format (written, audio, video, etc.). Below are reputable, widely trusted options categorized by use case, with context on their strengths and potential biases to help you choose:

### For neutral, fact-focused general news (minimal opinion/analysis)
- **Reuters / Associated Press (AP)**: These are global wire services that supply news to thousands of other outlets worldwide. They prioritize straight, verified facts over commentary, with very little institutional editorial slant, making them ideal for getting unvarnished updates on breaking and ongoing events. The main tradeoff is less in-depth feature or long-form analysis content compared to other outlets.

### For balanced general international news with diverse perspectives
- **BBC World Service**: Publicly funded by the UK's license fee, with a legal mandate for editorial impartiality. It offers extensive global coverage, including underreported stories from low-income regions, and is available in dozens of languages. Some critics note occasional Western or UK-centric bias in coverage of UK foreign policy, but it remains one of the most widely trusted general news sources globally.
- **Al Jazeera English**: Based in Qatar, it is widely praised for its focus on Global South perspectives, covering stories often overlooked by Western media (e.g., conflicts in Africa, labor rights in Southeast Asia, climate impacts in low-income countries). While its regional coverage of Middle Eastern affairs may reflect a slight pro-Qatar slant, its international reporting is rigorously fact-checked and far less Western-centric than most comparable Western outlets.
- For in-depth global analysis (rather than just breaking news):
  - *The Economist*: A centrist, well-researched outlet covering global politics, economics, and culture, though it is generally pro-free-market in its editorial stance.
  - *Financial Times*: The gold standard for business, economic, and financial news, with high-quality general reporting as well.

### For regional/local news
Your best option will almost always be a locally focused, independent outlet (e.g., public radio stations, local non-profit news organizations) that covers issues directly impacting your community. For example, local NPR affiliates in the U.S. often have strong community reporting; in many countries, independent local digital news outlets fill gaps left by corporate or state-owned media.
For national news in major markets, long-standing outlets like *The Guardian* (UK, left-leaning), *The Times* (UK, right-leaning), *Le Monde* (France, centrist), or *The New York Times* (U.S., centrist with a slight liberal slant in domestic coverage) all have high journalistic standards, though their editorial stances will be evident in opinion and analysis sections.

### For niche topic coverage
- Climate & environment: *Inside Climate News* (a non-profit exclusively focused on climate reporting) and *Carbon Brief* (data-driven, evidence-based climate coverage) are top choices.
- Investigative journalism: *ProPublica* (U.S. non-profit) and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (UK independent non-profit) produce deep, long-form investigative work on undercovered issues like corporate malfeasance, government corruption, and social inequality.
- Science & technology: *Nature* and *Science* are the leading peer-reviewed scientific journals for cutting-edge research, while outlets like *New Scientist*, Ars Technica, and *The Verge* offer accessible, accurate popular science and tech coverage for general audiences.

---

### Important media literacy note
No news outlet is completely free of bias—funding models (state-funded, corporate-owned, non-profit) and editorial missions will shape coverage. To get a well-rounded view:
1. Cross-reference breaking news across multiple independent outlets before forming conclusions, as initial reports are often incomplete or incorrect.
2. Be aware of an outlet's known slant, and seek out perspectives from outlets with differing stances on issues you care about.
3. Prioritize outlets with transparent editorial policies, clear fact-checking processes, and a track record of correcting errors when they occur.
4. Avoid outlets that rely heavily on clickbait, anonymous sourcing, or have repeatedly been flagged by independent fact-checkers for spreading misinformation. Note that social media algorithms often prioritize sensational, engagement-driven content over accurate reporting, so it is better to access news directly from outlets' official websites or apps rather than via social media feeds.

If you have specific needs (e.g., news in a certain language, coverage of a specific region or topic, a preferred format like podcasts or newsletters), feel free to share more details for more tailored recommendations.

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
There is no single "perfect" news outlet, as all editorial organizations have some inherent perspective, and journalistic standards vary widely. The most reliable way to stay informed is to cross-reference coverage of contentious or high-stakes topics across multiple sources, and prioritize outlets that clearly distinguish between factual reporting and labeled opinion/analysis.

That said, here are widely respected outlets known for strong fact-checking, transparency, and rigorous reporting, organized by use case:

### 1. Wire services (best for fast, minimally biased factual reporting)
The Associated Press (AP) and Reuters are independent, global wire services that supply news to thousands of local and national outlets worldwide. They prioritize straight, source-based reporting with almost no opinion commentary, have public error-correction policies, and are widely considered the gold standard for breaking news and factual baseline reporting.

### 2. General interest outlets with high journalistic standards
These outlets have dedicated news desks with strict sourcing rules, and clearly separate their factual reporting from labeled opinion sections:
- *BBC News*: UK publicly funded outlet with a global mandate, known for strict editorial impartiality guidelines for its straight news coverage, and broad international reporting that often includes undercovered Global South stories.
- *NPR (U.S.)*: U.S. public radio network with a strong track record of in-depth domestic and international investigative reporting, clear separation of news and commentary, and extensive local/regional coverage.
- *The New York Times*: U.S. mainstream outlet with a highly respected news desk known for investigative reporting and wide sourcing; its progressive opinion section is explicitly labeled as commentary, separate from its news content.
- *The Wall Street Journal*: U.S. outlet with a top-tier news desk particularly strong for business, economic, and domestic policy reporting; its conservative opinion section is clearly marked as commentary, separate from factual news coverage.
- *The Economist*: UK-based weekly magazine focused on in-depth analysis of global politics, economics, and business, with well-sourced reporting and a broadly liberal internationalist editorial stance (analysis is explicitly labeled as such).

Note that outlets with primarily opinion-driven programming (such as Fox News, or MSNBC’s prime-time commentary shows) are designed to cater to specific ideological perspectives rather than deliver neutral factual reporting, so they should be consumed with that context in mind, and not relied on as a primary source for news.

### 3. International and Global South-focused outlets
- *Al Jazeera English*: Qatar-funded outlet with exceptional coverage of underreported stories across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East that are often overlooked by Western media. Its straight news reporting is generally well-sourced, though critics note potential bias in coverage of topics tied to Qatari government interests.

### 4. Non-partisan fact-checking resources
For verifying claims from politicians, viral social media content, or partisan punditry, these independent, non-partisan outlets trace claims to original sources and publish transparent corrections:
- PolitiFact
- FactCheck.org
- AP Fact Check

### 5. Local and regional news
Don’t overlook local/regional outlets for coverage of hyper-local issues (city council decisions, school board policies, local infrastructure, community events) that national outlets almost never report on. Non-profit local newsrooms are often particularly reliable, as they are less reliant on corporate advertising or partisan funding.

---
### Tips for evaluating any news source:
- Prioritize outlets that clearly label opinion/analysis as separate from factual reporting, and avoid sources that blend the two without disclosure.
- Look for transparent error-correction policies: reputable outlets will publicly correct factual mistakes and note when a story has been updated with new information.
- Avoid outlets that rely on sensational, clickbait headlines, unsubstantiated anonymous sourcing, or consistently frame stories to provoke outrage rather than inform.
